segments.voice: Yesterday: Genesis 1, and the refrain that comes seven times. Your line was it was good. Did you stop and look at one finished thing? Day seven, the end of your first week.

A farm in the world of the Torah, on the seventh day. The family isn't working. Fine. But look closer. The hired hand isn't working either. The foreign worker who lives at the edge of the village is sitting in the shade. And the ox, the one that pulls the plow six days a week, is standing in the field doing absolutely nothing, and nobody is allowed to put it to work. And one law wrote the animals in, by name. Today, at the end of week one: the commandment that rests everyone.
screen: `A FARM ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` → `THE WORKER RESTS.` → `EVEN THE OX RESTS.`

segments.voice: The Sabbath commandment is one of the Ten Words given at Sinai, the fourth in the Jewish count. It appears twice in the Torah, in two slightly different versions, and the difference is the lesson. In Exodus it begins: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And the reason given is creation: in six days God made the world, and on the seventh God rested. Rest is built into the world itself, right after the six days of making we met yesterday. In Deuteronomy, Moses repeats it, and it begins: "Observe the sabbath day, to keep it holy." This time the reason is different. It's Egypt. You were slaves, so rest: "that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest as well as thou." As well as you. Not after you. Not instead of you. The same. Both versions list who rests: you, your son, your daughter, the servants, the stranger in your town, and the animals. Another law in Exodus puts it more plainly still, rest on the seventh day, "that thine ox and thine ass may have rest." The rabbis read those two versions as one. Remember and observe, they said, were spoken in a single utterance, the way only God could say two things at once. That's the two candles from day four. And so rest here isn't a treat you earn once your work is done. It's owed to everyone, and especially to whoever works for you.
screen: `REMEMBER — BECAUSE OF CREATION.` · `OBSERVE — BECAUSE OF EGYPT.` · `AS WELL AS THOU.` · `THE OX AND THE ASS REST TOO.` · then, large: `REST IS OWED.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell, and a look back at your first week: shalom, the Shema, Shabbat, the candles, bracha, Genesis one, and today. On the first breath, think of someone who works so your life runs, a driver, a cleaner, a parent. On the second, wish them a real rest. On the third, give yourself one too.
The Sabbath commandment. Remember, and observe: rest, for you, your household, the stranger and even the animals. Seventh word. A full week.
Your line: rest is for everyone. Today, make someone else's load lighter by one thing: a thank you, a task you take off them, an early finish. Day seven. Week one, done.

howItsDone: Jews read both versions of the Ten Commandments in the yearly Torah cycle, and the Friday-night hymn Lecha Dodi speaks in its first verse of remember and observe being said as one word.

myth: the Sabbath commandment appears only once in the Torah
twice: remember in Exodus, observe in Deuteronomy.
the ox and the donkey rest with the household.
the two versions give the same reason
Exodus points to creation; Deuteronomy points to slavery in Egypt.

fork.setup: in Deuteronomy, Moses repeats the Sabbath commandment. what reason does he give for the servants' rest?
options: because you were slaves in Egypt.
fork.reveal: Egypt: you were slaves once, so your servants rest "as well as thou."

original.note: Hebrew: remember and observe, the opening words of the two versions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about going to worship.
what it means: a rest owed to everyone in the house, down to the servants, the stranger and the ox.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 20 grounds it in creation, Deuteronomy 5 in the exodus. the rabbis taught both were spoken in one utterance, a line Lecha Dodi sings on Friday night.
